title: Docetism: Christ Only Seemed Human
lead: Docetism is the teaching that Christ only seemed to have a real human body, or only seemed to suffer and die. The name comes from Greek dokein, 'to seem'. The New Testament already tests teachers by whether they confess 'Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh' (1 John 4:2), and the letters of Ignatius of Antioch, early in the second century, fight teachers who said Christ suffered 'only in appearance' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1). The opposite belief, that the Son of God truly became human, is on the page The Incarnation.

sections.h: 'Come in the flesh': the test in John's letters
sections.b: John's letters give a test for teachers: 'any spirit that confesses Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is from God' (1 John 4:2), 'and any spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God' (1 John 4:3). 'For many deceivers went out into the world, people who do not confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh. This one is the deceiver and the antichrist' (2 John 7). The letters do not name the teachers or give their arguments. The Catholic Encyclopedia's article on the Docetae says that 'Beyond doubt St. John ... refers to this heresy', citing Dionysius of Alexandria (in Eusebius, Church History 7.25) and Tertullian. The letters themselves name only the confession they require.

Kirsopp Lake describes the teaching Ignatius fought as 'docetism (δοκεῖν), which regarded the sufferings, and in some cases the life, of Jesus as merely an appearance'. The name as a label for a group came later. The Catholic Encyclopedia (Arendzen, 1909) says the word 'Docetae' 'first occurs in a letter of Serapion, Bishop of Antioch (190-203)', about the Gospel of Peter, and then in Clement of Alexandria (Stromata 3.13 and 7.17); it adds that Docetism, 'as far as at present known', always went with Gnostic or later Manichaean systems, which held that matter could not belong to the highest God. Ancient writers report forms of it in Basilides, Cerdo, Marcion and Valentinus, as the article summarizes from Irenaeus, Tertullian and Hippolytus.
sections.refs: 1 John 4:2-3; 2 John 7; Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 2:1

sections.h: The answer of the early churches
sections.b: Ignatius answers with history: Christ was 'truly born of a virgin', 'truly nailed' under Pontius Pilate, truly raised, and in the flesh after the resurrection (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 1:1-3:3). If his suffering was only an appearance, Ignatius says, 'then I too am in chains only in appearance' (Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans 4:2). Polycarp, overseer of Smyrna, repeats John's test: 'everyone who does not confess Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh is an antichrist' (Polycarp to the Philippians 7:1).
